howTo: Enter working pressure, bore diameter, rod diameter, and available flow with the units shown by the calculator.
Compare extend force against the full bore area and retract force against the annulus area.
Use the speed and ideal-power results as a circuit screening check, then add real pressure losses and efficiency effects.
formula: A_bore = pi D^2 / 4 | A_annulus = pi (D^2 - d^2) / 4 | F_extend = p A_bore | F_retract = p A_annulus | v = Q / A | P_hydraulic = p Q

examples.title: 80 / 45 mm cylinder at 160 bar
examples.description: An original sizing example for checking the difference between extending and retracting performance.
notes: Retract speed is higher because flow passes through the smaller annulus area.
The displayed force is theoretical. Seal friction, back pressure, leakage, and line losses reduce available force.

examples.title: 100 / 50 mm cylinder at 200 bar
examples.description: A second check to compare the effect of a larger bore and flow rate.
notes: Check rod buckling, end mounting, valve capacity, hose rating, and system safety separately before selecting hardware.

references.title: ISO 4413
references.note: Hydraulic fluid power safety requirements and system guidance; consult the current licensed edition.

references.title: Cylinder and valve manufacturer data
references.note: Confirm pressure rating, seals, friction, allowable side load, speed limits, and mounting arrangement with supplier data.

commonMistakes: Entering a rod diameter equal to or larger than the bore diameter.
Reading theoretical force as net force at the load after valve, hose, and back-pressure losses.
Comparing flow values without converting L/min consistently when checking another calculation.
assumptions: Pressure is treated as constant and the fluid as incompressible for this baseline calculation.
The model does not resolve dynamic pressure spikes, leakage, seal friction, compressibility, or circuit transients.
Final hydraulic-component selection requires the complete circuit and safety assessment.
